title: Sinus Elevation Implants Had 94.3% Estimated 5-Year Survival; Approach Comparison Unclear
html:
Implants placed after maxillary sinus floor elevation had an estimated survival rate of 94.29% at five years and 92.85% at 10 years, according to a retrospective cohort study published Nov. 15 in Maxillofacial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery. A comparison of lateral and crestal approaches did not produce a firm conclusion.

The single-center study included 527 implants placed in 212 patients between January 2003 and April 2018, with records reviewed through Nov. 10, 2025. Failure was defined as implant removal or spontaneous loss.

Twenty-seven implants failed in 19 patients. Median observed follow-up was 28.7 months, and 191 implants remained at risk at five years and 87 at 10 years. Follow-up completeness was 53.8% at five years and 41.7% at 10 years.

In the pooled analysis, crestal procedures carried a higher hazard of failure than lateral procedures, with a hazard ratio of 3.48 (robust 95% CI, 1.50–8.10; P = .0037). A patient-level bootstrap analysis produced a wider 95% CI of 0.82–7.94.

Eight of the nine crestal failures occurred among implants placed from 2003 through 2007. Among implants placed from 2008 through 2018, only one crestal implant failed, and the hazard ratio was 0.52 (95% CI, 0.06–4.73; P = .5595).

The authors concluded that incomplete follow-up limits interpretation of the survival estimates, particularly at 10 years. Because of unmeasured confounding and uncertainty, they said, the pooled difference between approaches cannot be attributed to surgical technique or to a learning effect. The exploratory later-period results do not establish that the approaches are equivalent.

The study was conducted by Min Hyung Choi, Kwang Jun Kwon, and Young Wook Park of the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at Kangwon National University in Gangneung, South Korea. The authors declared no competing interests.

Sources:
